The paper "Parallelizing Linear Transformers with the Delta Rule over Sequence Length" was authored by Yang, S., Wang, B., Zhang, Y., Shen, Y., & Kim, Y. (2024) and published in the Proceedings of the 38th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2024).

The arXiv identifier is 2406.06484, which matches your query.

## Paper Summary

The work describes a hardware-efficient algorithm for training linear transformers with the delta rule, which exploits a memory-efficient representation for computing products of Householder matrices, allowing the team to scale up DeltaNet to standard language modeling settings.

## Research Context

While more expressive variants of linear transformers which replace the additive update in linear transformers with the delta rule (DeltaNet) have been found to be more effective at associative recall, existing algorithms for training such models do not parallelize over sequence length and are thus inefficient to train on modern hardware.

The paper was presented in the NeurIPS 2024 Main Conference Track, and it was published as a poster presentation on September 25, 2024.

"Predictive Multiplicity in Classification" by Charles Marx, Flavio du Pin Calmon, and Berk Ustun was published at ICML 2020.

The paper defines predictive multiplicity as the ability of a prediction problem to admit competing models with conflicting predictions, and introduces measures to evaluate the severity of predictive multiplicity, along with integer programming tools to compute these measures exactly for linear classification problems.

The authors applied their tools to measure predictive multiplicity in recidivism prediction problems and found that real-world datasets may admit competing models that assign wildly conflicting predictions.

The paper is available in several formats, including on the MLPR proceedings at https://proceedings.mlr.press/v119/marx20a.html and on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.06677.

## Paper Details

"Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding" is a paper by Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Steven Basart, Andy Zou, Mantas Mazeika, Dawn Song, and Jacob Steinhardt published at ICLR 2021.

## What the Paper Introduces

The paper proposes a new test to measure a text model's multitask accuracy, covering 57 tasks including elementary mathematics, US history, computer science, law, and more. To attain high accuracy on this test, models must possess extensive world knowledge and problem solving ability.

## Key Findings

While most recent models have near random-chance accuracy, the very largest GPT-3 model improves over random chance by almost 20 percentage points on average. However, on every one of the 57 tasks, the best models still need substantial improvements before they can reach expert-level accuracy. Models also have lopsided performance and frequently do not know when they are wrong, with near-random accuracy on some socially important subjects such as morality and law.

## Resources

The official repository is available at GitHub (hendrycks/test), and the benchmark dataset is also hosted on Hugging Face.

The authors are Songlin Yang, Bailin Wang, Yikang Shen, Rameswar Panda, and Yoon Kim.

The work describes a hardware-efficient algorithm for linear attention that trades off memory movement against parallelizability. The resulting implementation, dubbed FlashLinearAttention, is faster than FlashAttention-2 as a standalone layer even on short sequence lengths (e.g., 1K).

Transformers with linear attention allow for efficient parallel training but can be formulated as an RNN with 2D (matrix-valued) hidden states, thus enjoying linear-time inference complexity. However, linear attention generally underperforms ordinary softmax attention. Moreover, current implementations of linear attention lack I/O-awareness and are thus slower than highly optimized implementations of softmax attention.
